title: Floating and Sinking Boats
strapline: Build a boat from whatever is on the table, then find out the hard way whether it floats.
intent: Children explore scientific concepts — floating, sinking, materials — through water play.
Predicting before testing is the beginning of real scientific method.
A boat that sinks is a genuine problem to solve, and children want to solve it.
Comparing materials builds understanding of properties: heavy, light, waterproof.
Water play sustains long, absorbed investigation better than almost anything else.
implementation: Provide different materials — plastic, foil, wood, sponge, card — for children to make boats.
Ask for a prediction before each test: do you think it will float or sink?
Test them in a water tray deep enough that sinking is unambiguous.
Model the vocabulary as they work: float, sink, heavy, light, waterproof, soggy.
When a boat sinks, ask what they could change rather than supplying the answer.
Add cargo — pennies, pebbles, small figures — so children test how much a boat can hold.
Record findings on a simple float/sink chart the children fill in themselves.
key_questions: Do you think it will float or sink? Why?
What happened? Was that what you expected?
How could you change your boat so it floats better?
How many pennies can your boat carry before it sinks?
Which material made the best boat, and why do you think that is?

impact.text: Children explore forces, materials and change through play.
Children make predictions, test them, and still ask why.
Children build and construct with purpose and tell you about it.
Children compare amounts and sizes — heavier, lighter, more, full, empty.
Children keep trying when a first attempt fails.
Children take up and use new scientific vocabulary.

enhancements: A boat-building challenge — whose boat can carry the most cargo?
A water tray outdoors with guttering and a current to sail the boats down.
A sink-or-float sorting station with everyday objects, away from the making.
A junk-modelling table so boats can be designed properly before testing.
A story link with a boat or sea-journey picture book beside the tray.
A photograph record of each design and what happened to it.

playing_exploring: Children choose materials freely and build whatever they think will work.
Water play invites long, absorbed, open-ended investigation.
active_learning: Children rebuild and retest after a failure rather than giving up.
They stay at the water tray for extended stretches.
creating_thinking: Children predict, test and revise — the whole scientific loop.
They reason about why one material behaved differently from another.
